title: Highly Efficient CO2 Reduction on Ordered Porous Cu Electrode Derived from Cu2O Inverse Opals
abstract: Electrochemical reduction of CO2 to fuels is a promising way to reduce CO2 emission and address the environment and energy crisis. However, the H2 evolution reaction competes with CO2 electrochemical reduction, which would lower the overall efficiency for carbonaceous products. In this work, a new electrocatalyst (cubic-shaped Cu inverse opals) was reported to reduce CO2 to useful chemicals, which was synthesized from an electrochemical reduction of Cu2O inverse opals. The Cu inverse opals could electrochemically reduce CO2 to CO and HCOOH with a Faradaic 2 efficiency of 45.3% and 33.6 %, which was 3 times and 5 times higher than that of Cu particles film at identical conditions. The improved Faradaic efficiency for CO2 reduction was ascribed to the enhanced stabilization for the CO2• − intermediate on the high surface area of Cu inverse opals, and the greatly improved reactant diffusion in this interconnected and ordered macroporous structure. The design of Cu inverse opals presents a prospective application of inverse opals in CO2 reduction through constructing inverse-opal structure as groundwork, which may provide key structure−activity insights for efficient CO2 reduction.

sections.text:
Electrochemical reduction of CO2 to fuels is a promising way to reduce CO2 emission and address the environment and energy crisis. However, the H2 evolution reaction competes with CO2 electrochemical reduction, which would lower the overall efficiency for carbonaceous products. In
this work, a new electrocatalyst (cubic-shaped Cu inverse opals) was reported to reduce CO2 to useful chemicals, which was synthesized from an electrochemical reduction of Cu2O inverse opals. The Cu inverse opals could electrochemically reduce CO2 to CO and HCOOH with a Faradaic
efficiency of 45.3% and 33.6 %, which was 3 times and 5 times higher than that of Cu particles film
at identical conditions. The improved Faradaic efficiency for CO2 reduction was ascribed to the enhanced stabilization for the CO2• − intermediate on the high surface area of Cu inverse opals, and the greatly improved reactant diffusion in this interconnected and ordered macroporous structure.
The design of Cu inverse opals presents a prospective application of inverse opals in CO2 reduction through constructing inverse-opal structure as groundwork, which may provide key
structure−activity insights for efficient CO2 reduction.
Keywords: electrochemical reduction; inverse opals; Faradaic efficiency; CO; HCOOH

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text:
Although coal, oil, natural gas and other hydrocarbon fuels provide indispensable energy for
society’s energy demands, their mining, refining and use result in considerable greenhouse gas
emissions (main component is CO2) and other significant environmental problems. The rapidly increase in carbon emissions breaks the balance of the carbon cycle in nature, leading to a steady
increase in the concentration of CO2-dominated greenhouse gases in the atmosphere. [1, 2] How to control CO2 concentration and deal with the energy crisis, is a major research topic for governments and scientists. [3-6] A great deal of effort has been expended to reduce the CO2 concentration in the atmosphere [7-13], and catalysis is an extremely attractive approach to converting CO2 into industrially relevant chemicals and fuels. [14-17] CO2 as a valuable resource can be catalytically by thermochemical, photochemical, and electrochemical and other methods. Electrochemical reduction
is a promising strategy because it operates with high reaction rates and good efficiencies under
ambient conditions, uses environmentally benign aqueous electrolytes, and easily couples with
carbon-free electricity sources (e.g., wind, solar, hydroelectric, etc.). [18, 19]
In CO2 electrochemical reduction, researchers have identified various electrocatalytic materials in CO2-saturated aqueous solutions. [20-24] Among currently identified catalyst materials, many studies have concentrated on Cu electrodes because Cu can reduce CO2 to CO and hydrocarbons, such as CH4, C2H4, CH3OH and HCOOH. [25-30] There are some reports of Cu electrodes made into
different morphologies, such as porous [31-34], nanowires [35-37], foams [38, 39], and ribbon arrays
[40], etc., exhibiting better catalytic activity and higher product selectivity in CO2 reduction. Inverse opal (IO) structure has three-dimensional interconnected frame and interconnected spherical
channels, which are favorable for the dynamic diffusion of the reactant molecules, promoting the
adsorption and activation of CO2 on the electrodes. The gold inverse-opal (Au-IO) thin films were active for CO2 reduction to CO with high efficiency at modest overpotentials and high selectivity relative to hydrogen evolution. [41] Moreover, well-defined mesostructured silver inverse opal
(Ag-IO) electrodes demonstrated that mesostructure-induced transport limitations alone served to
increase the turnover frequency for CO2 activation per unit area, while simultaneously improving reaction selectivity. [42] The specific activity for catalyzed CO evolution systematically rose by
three-fold and the specific activity for catalyzed H2 evolution systematically declined by ten-fold with increasing mesostructural roughness of Ag-IOs. All the above studies indicate that inverse opal
structure plays an important role in the catalytic activity and selectivity of CO2 electrochemical reduction. However, there are few reports focused on Cu inverse opal (Cu-IO) electrodes in CO2 electrochemical reduction.
For inverse opal electrocatalysts, one of the most important properties is the periodic structure
with high surface/volume fractions and interconnected pores. This structure can offer a large internal
surface area, supplying lots of reaction active sites, which is beneficial for the CO2 adsorption and reduction. Herein, we show the performance of CO2 electrochemical reduction on Cu-IOs derived from Cu2O-IOs for the first time. Cu-IOs could electrochemically reduce CO2 to useful fuels, with significantly higher Faradaic efficiencies (FEs) of CO and HCOOH than Cu particles film. Finally,
the reduction mechanism over Cu-IOs was discussed.

sections.heading: 2.1 Materials
sections.text:
All solvents and chemicals were of reagent quality. Styrene (Aldrich, 99%) and K2S2O8 (AR, Sinopharm Chemical Reagent Co., China) were used to prepare polystyrene (PS) opal templates
(Detailed experiments see in Supporting information). CuSO4, lactic acid, NaOH, and tetrahydrofuran (AR, Sinopharm Chemical Reagent Co., China) were used to prepare Cu2O-IOs.

sections.heading: 2.2 Synthesis of Cu2O inverse opal thin films
sections.text:
The Cu2O inversal opal films were prepared by electrochemical reduction of copper(II) lactate in alkaline solution. [43] The electrolyte solution was composed of 0.4 M CuSO4 and 3 M lactic acid, and the pH value of the solution was adjusted to 12 by 10 wt % NaOH solution. Cu2O-IOs and Cu2O particles were grown with constant potential in a three-electrode system, which was controlled by a CHI660E electrochemical system (Chenhua Instruments Co., China). PS template (1.0 × 2.0 cm 2 ) on FTO film (1.0 × 5.0 × 0.2 cm 3 ) was used as the working electrode, and a copper wire used as the
counter electrode, with a saturated calomel electrode (SCE) as the reference electrode. The
electrochemical deposition was performed at −0.7 V vs. SCE for 20 minutes, and the temperature was kept at 45 o C. Herein, Cu2O precursor was grown into the voids of PS template usig this method. After immersed into the tetrahydrofuran for several minutes, the PS template was removed while
simultaneously forming the Cu2O inverse opal framework. At last, the film was calcined at 500 °C in N2 for 2 hours with a heating rate of 2 °C/min. Correspondingly, Cu2O particles without porous structure was synthesized on the bare FTO substrate, and the method was same to Cu2O-IOs.

sections.heading: 2.3 Characterization of Samples
sections.text:
The surface morphologies and structure of CuO-IO and Cu-IO samples were characterized by
using scanning electron microscope (SEM) on a Sigma Zeiss 150 instrument (Carl Zeiss Co.,
Germany). The crystal structure of CuO-IO and Cu-IO samples was determined from X‐ ray
diffraction (XRD) patterns recorded on a Bruker D8 Advance X-ray diffractometer with Cu Kα
radiation (λ = 0.154 nm, scan rate of 4°/min). The microscope images were collected by Olympus
microscopes (BX53, Olympus Co., Japan). X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (PHI5300, Perkin
Elmer Co., USA) was investigated with monochromatic Mg Kα radiation, and all the binding
energies were referenced to the C1s peak at 284.6 eV.

sections.heading: 2.4 Electrochemical measurement
sections.text:
CO2 reduction experiments were performed in an electrochemical reactor (Figure S1, Supporting Information), comprised of three electrodes, which were separated by proton exchange membrane
into two compartment cells (working and counter electrode compartments). The reactor was made
from Teflon and separated by proton exchange membrane (Nafion-117) to prevent the oxidation of
CO2 reduction products. In the testing system, a piece of Cu2O-IO or Cu2O particles film was used as working electrodes with the size of 1.0 × 2.0 cm 2 , and Ag/AgCl was used as the reference electrode,
with Pt wire as the counter electrode. The applied potentials (vs. Ag/AgCl) were changed into the reversible hydrogen electrode (RHE) with the equation: VRHE = VAg/AgCl + V 0 Ag/AgCl vs. NHE + 0.059 pH, where V 0
Ag/AgCl vs. NHE is 0.199 V at 25 °C. [35]
The CO2 electrochemical reaction was performed at ambient temperature and pressure. In order to remove oxygen, high purity CO2 gas (purity 99.995%) was flowed through the electrolyte solution to achieve CO2 saturation before each experiment. The electrochemical experiment of CO2 was investigated in a 0.1 M KHCO3 electrolyte saturated with CO2 (pH = 6.8). The gaseous products produced during catalytic reduction of CO2 were collected and analyzed off line by a gas chromatograph instrument (GC-2014, Shimadzu Co., Japan). The liquid products formed during the
testing were analyzed off line using High Performance Liquid Chromatography (HPLC)
(Prominence HPLC, Shimadzu Co., Japan). The performance of CO2 reduction is evaluated by the FE (i.e., activity and selectivity of the reaction to produce CO and HCOOH). FE is calculated

sections.heading: 3. Results and discussion
sections.text:
3.1 Fabrication of Cu2O-IOs electrode
Scheme 1. Illustration of synthetic strategy: (a) PS template is formed by evaporation-induced
self-assembly. (b) The precursor is infiltrated, and (c) the template is removed to form Cu2O inverse opal structure.
The preparation of inverse-opal Cu2O electrodes is illustrated in Scheme 1. First, PS template is formed on top of the FTO surface by evaporation-induced self-assembly (morphology of the formed
template is shown in Figure 1). Electrochemical deposition is employed to infiltrate the Cu2O precursor into the voids of PS template. After immersed into the tetrahydrofuran for several minutes,
the template is removed with Cu2O inverse opal framework simultaneously formed.
As shown in Figure 1a, the PS template is obtained by the vertical deposition method, which
perform three-dimensional ordered structures. The PS template is denoted as PS360 as the average
size of PS sphere is 360 nm. Moreover, due to Bragg reflection, PS template surface exhibits
gorgeous color from different angle, demonstrating that PS template possesses highly ordered
structure. The photonic band gap of PS360 is shown in Figure 1b, and the absorption peak
(correspondingly 865 nm) is obviously observed, indicating the PS template well long-range
ordering.

Fig 2. (a) low-magnification and (b) high-magnification SEM images of Cu2O-IOs, (c) XRD pattern of Cu2O-IOs, and (d) SEM image of Cu2O particles.
After immersion and calcination processes, it can be observed that Cu2O-IOs are well duplicated the PS template to form an ordered skeleton structure from SEM images (Figure 2a and 2b). The
skeleton structure is composed of periodical interconnected macropores. For comparison,
electrochemical deposition is also performed to obtain Cu2O particles film on FTO without colloidal crystal template. The SEM images of Cu2O particles film are shown in Figure 2d and Figure S2. Cu2O particles show regular cubic morphology, and are well dispersed on the surface of FTO. While the electrochemical deposition is performed with colloidal crystal template on FTO, Cu2O only grow in the void of the template. Therefore, after removing the template, Cu2O particles with three dimensional ordered macroporous structure and cubic morphology are obtained, and the 6-micron
cube-like structures is influenced by the shape of Cu2O particles. Under higher magnification, it is confirmed that every Cu2O crystal is composed of hexagonally ordered pores with diameter of 340 nm (Figure 2b), which is comparable with the size of PS spheres (360 nm). Optical microscope
images of the as-prepared Cu2O-IOs are also investigated and shown in Figure S3, and the electrode with uniform and a big area of Cu2O-IOs is observed.
The typical XRD patterns of the Cu2O-IOs and particles film on FTO substrate are shown in Figure 2c and S4, respectively. All peaks of the prepared Cu2O-IOs and Cu2O particles matches well with the standard Cu2O crystal phase (JCPDS No. 05-0667). Five distinguishable peaks of 29.6°, 36.4°, 42.3°, 61.3° and 73.5° are respectively corresponding to (110), (111), (200), (220) and (311)
crystal planes of Cu2O. It suggests that the Cu2O-IOs and Cu2O particles are successfully prepared.

sections.heading: 3.2 Fabrication of Cu-IOs derived from Cu2O-IOs.
sections.text:
The resulted Cu2O-IOs is then electrochemically reduced to Cu-IOs electrodes in CO2 reduction. To confirm the component of the Cu-IOs after electrochemical reduction, SEM, XRD and XPS data
were then measured. The SEM images of Cu2O-IOs after electrochemical reduction at −0.6 V vs. RHE performs that inverse-opal structure is retained, which is exhibited in Figure 3a (a SEM image
under higher magnification is provided). The Cu particles electrode is prepared under identical
condition after electrochemical reduction of Cu2O particles electrode. The smooth surface of cubic-shaped Cu2O particles is roughened due to the electrochemical reduction (Figure 3b).
To further study the electrochemical reduction process of Cu2O-IO, the XRD pattern of Cu2O-IO after 10 min of electrochemical reduction is provided in Figure S5. The coexistence of Cu2O and Cu is observed, indicating that Cu2O are partially converted to Cu. However, when the electrochemical process last 90 min, the peak of Cu2O (36.8°) disappeared (Figure 3c), only peaks from Cu 0 and FTO are observed, suggesting that all the oxides are reduced to Cu. Additionally, XPS spectra were
measured to investigate the states of Cu2O-IOs before and after CO2 reduction experiments. For Cu2O-IOs sample, high-resolution spectrum of Cu 2p (Figure 3d) displays the characteristic peaks of 932.57 eV (Cu 2p3/2) and 952.44 eV (Cu 2p1/2) corresponding to chemical element state of Cu 1+ (Cu2O). [35, 44] After electrochemical reduction, the Cu 2p3/2 peak shifts to 932.47 eV. Although there is a little shift and some broadening, it is still difficult to discriminate the attribution of this Cu 2p3/2 peak (Cu 2+ , Cu 1+ or Cu 0 ). Because Cu 1+ is not so stable when sample is taken out of the solution, it may generate CuO. According to the XRD data, Cu is the main product in the sample
after electrochemical reduction, and thus Cu-IOs is used as the electrode to reduce CO2 into valuable hydrocarbon fuels.

sections.heading: 3.3 CO2 Reduction performance on Cu2O-derived Cu-IOs
sections.text:
The electrochemical performances of Cu-IOs and Cu particles in CO2-saturated 0.1 M KHCO3 electrolytes are investigated and presented in Figure 4. Current densities of Cu-IOs and Cu particles
electrodes are measured, which is a function of applied potential and demonstrate the electron
generation capacity and electron transfer effectiveness. The currents of Cu-IOs and Cu particles are
investigated (Figure 4a), which increase with the increasing of applied negative potentials. Obviously,
the current of Cu-IOs is much higher than that of Cu particles at the same potentials. For example, at
−0.6 V vs. RHE, the enhancement factor is 64%, confirming that the Cu inverse-opal structure can
achieve higher catalytic activity. CO2 reduction activity on Cu2O-derived Cu-IOs and Cu particles film at −0.6 V vs. RHE are investigated and exhibited in Figure 4b. It is observed that the Cu-IOs not
only exhibit a much higher current density (1.2 mA/cm 2 ), but higher FE for CO reduction (45.3%)
than that of Cu particles film (14.6%).
Fig 4. (a) Steady-state total current densities at various potentials for Cu-IOs and Cu particles. (b) CO2 reduction activity on Cu2O-derived Cu-IOs and Cu particles film at -0.6 V vs. RHE in CO2-saturated 0.1 M KHCO3 electrolytes (inset is the CO FEs for Cu-IOs and Cu particles).
To further evaluate the catalytic activity of CO2 reduction, the product generation rates (Figure 5a and 5b), carbon atom conversion rates (Figure 5c), and FEs (Figure 5d) on Cu-IOs and Cu particles
are studied and compared. During the electrochemical reduction, the main products are HCOOH, CO and H2. The highest carbon atom conversion rate is 13.2 μmol/(h·cm 2 ) for Cu particles at -1.0 V vs. RHE, much lower than that of Cu-IOs [69.0 μmol/(h·cm 2 )] (Figure 5c). The outstanding catalytic
activity of Cu-IOs mainly ascribes to its high reactant absorptivity and efficient charge transportation.
The FEs of hydrocarbon products on Cu-IOs and Cu particles at varying bias are summarized and
shown in Figure 5d. For Cu particles film, when the potential is less negative than −0.4 V vs. RHE,
the current density is low and the amount products of CO2 reduction is small. However, at this potential, the Cu-IOs revealed a FE of 28.0% for CO production and 21.7 % for HCOOH production.
The FEs of CO production on Cu-IOs are firstly increased and then declined with the increasing
potentials, which reach a maximum at −0.6 V. The highest FE for CO production is 45.3 %, which is
3 times higher than that of Cu particles. The FE of HCOOH on Cu-IOs also exhibit a similar trend
and reach a maximum at −0.8 V vs. RHE. The CO generation rate at −0.6 V is 5 times faster than
The previous reports have also demonstrated that the Cu electrode with different morphology
possessed high activity and sensitivity in CO2 reduction reaction. For instance, Cu nanocubes exhibited the high selectivity towards CO2 reduction reaction (80%) and faradaic efficiency for ethylene (41%). [29] Cu nanowire arrays can electrochemically reduce CO2 to CO with a faradaic efficiency of ~50%. [35] Moreover, the faradaic efficiency of HCOOH produced at copper foam
electrodes was higher at all potentials with a maximum efficiency of 37%. [38] In our study, Cu
inverse opals can electrochemically reduce CO2 to CO and HCOOH with a faradaic efficiency of 45.3% and 33.6 %, and the total faradaic efficiency added up to 79%, which are comparable with
reported values on efficient Cu nanostructures.
Fig 6. The currents of Cu-IOs and Cu particles during 10 hours of CO2 electrochemical reduction (inset is the corresponding SEM image of Cu-IOs).
Moreover, the stability of Cu-IOs is also evaluated with reaction time in terms of performing the
CO2 conversion (shown in Figure 6). The stability for Cu-IOs and Cu particles is investigated and characterized by SEM measurement (Figure S6 and S7). As the reaction proceeds, the current of
Cu-IOs only slightly decreases after 10 hrs in the experiment, implying the high stability of the
Cu-IOs electrode. Meanwhile, the inverse opal structure still exists, indicating the stability of the
structure. The morphology of Cu particles is slightly changed with some pores formed on the
surface after 10 hrs reaction, which could be attributed to the restructuring of the Cu surface during
electrochemical reaction.

sections.heading: 3.4. Possible Mechanism in CO2 electrochemical reduction
sections.text:
To obtain insight into the mechanistic pathways for CO2 reduction with Cu-IOs, the Tafel plot of overpotential vs. log(jCO) is investigated and shown in Figure 7, where jCO is the partial current density for CO production. The plot for Cu-IOs is linear over the range of overpotentials from 0.3 to
0.5 V with a slope of 91 mV/decade. The Tafel slope for Cu particle is 120 mV/decade, which is
consistent with a rate determining initial electron transfer to CO2 to form a surface adsorbed CO2•―
intermediate (116 mV/decade), and a mechanism that is commonly invoked for metal electrodes [44]
The dramatic difference in FE between the two electrodes suggests that the Cu surfaces formed by reducing Cu2O-IOs enable formation of the CO2• − intermediate while suppressing H2O reduction.

To determine the reaction order with respect to HCO3 − , electrolysis is performed at a constant applied potential at HCO3 − concentrations ranging from 0.05 to 0.3 M, with KClO4 added to the electrolyte to maintain ionic strength. [45, 46] A plot of log(jCO) vs log([HCO3 − ]) (Figure S8) exhibits a slope of 1.27, indicating that the donation of a proton from HCO3 − is the rate-determining
step for CO2 reduction on Cu-IOs surfaces. Therefore, a more likely scenario is that the rate-determining step is the protonation of CO2• − intermediate and the surface migration of HCO3 − to the surface sites inside the pores of Cu-IOs. With high intrinsic activity, extremely large surface area
and superior stability, Cu-IOs represents the excellent copper-based electrocatalyst reported for CO2 electroreduction to CO and HCOOH in aqueous electrolyte.
Scheme 2. Proposed mechanism for CO2 reduction to CO and HCOOH on Cu2O-derived Cu-IOs.
（The symbol “*” represents the surface）
It is generally accepted that the first electron transfer for the formation of the CO2• − is the rate determining step in the electrochemical reduction of CO2 to CO because the first electron transfer requires a much more negative potential compared to the following steps. [44] Tafel slope on Cu particles indicates the rate-determining initial e − transfer to CO2 to form an adsorbed CO2• − intermediate (equation 2). In contrast, electrokinetic data for Cu2O-derived Cu IOs support a mechanism that involves a facile e − transfer to CO2 to form adsorbed CO2• − (equation 2) followed by a rate determining H + transfer with HCO3 − serving as the H + donor. [14, 45] The more active sites provided by Cu-IOs may lead to the enhanced stabilization of the CO2• − . Subsequent relatively fast steps involving additional e − and H + transfers complete the reduction to CO (equation 3 and 5) and
HCOOH (equation 6). Mechanistic divergence from the rate-determining step suggests that active sites on the surfaces of Cu-IOs provide better stabilization for CO2• − than the sites on Cu particles film. There are mainly two reasons responsible for this result: one is that the high surface/volume
fractions and interconnected pores for inverse-opal electrocatalyst can provide more active sites and
facilitate the diffusion of reactants, and the other is that Cu-IOs possess higher reactant absorptivity
and more efficient charge transportation than Cu particles. The proposed mechanism (Scheme 2) for
Cu-IOs and detailed formulas of CO2 reduction are thus summarized as following: CO2 + e − CO2• − (2) CO2• − + e − + 2H + CO + H2O (3)
CO2• − + H + HCOO• (4) HCOO• + e −
CO + H2O (5)
HCOO • + e − + H + HCOOH (6)
Conclusions
Cubic-shaped Cu-IOs with a large area was fabricated from Cu2O-IOs through an electrochemical reduction method. In the electrochemical reduction, Cu-IOs can selectively reduce CO2 to CO and HCOOH with high Faradaic efficiencies at a moderate potential. This high activity and selectivity in
CO2 reduction may be due to the high surface/volume fractions and interconnected pores of Cu-IOs, which provide more active sites and dramatically improve the stabilization of CO2• − intermediates. In this study, Cu inverse opals as a novel electrode structure may provide another approach to
influencing the catalytic sensitivity during CO2 reduction, and offer a prospective application through constructing structure for efficient CO2 reduction.
